findings.title: Debug logging left at Error level, dumping full ID lists every batch
findings.body: Each cleanup batch logs at Error level with the full slice of fetched IDs, the SQL condition and a nil error. This happens at lines 534/537 (by time), 554/557 (by count) and 576/579 (orphaned tags). With batch sizes up to tens of thousands, every batch writes huge log lines. Healthy runs will flood the logs and trigger error-based alerting. The final no-op batch also logs at Error level. These look like leftover debugging statements and should be removed or lowered to Debug without the ID list.

findings.title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The ticker for all cleanup jobs went from 10 minutes to 1 minute, while each run still has a 9-minute timeout. This affects snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history and annotations. It is unrelated to the deadlock fix, is not mentioned in the PR description, and looks like a leftover local testing change. It multiplies DB load by 10x and makes contention with the annotation write path more likely, which works against the stated goal of reducing deadlocks. Revert it.

findings.title: Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
findings.body: The SQLite inline path builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so the cost is O(n^2). This path only runs when the batch size exceeds 999, i.e. for large batches such as the 32767 used in the test, so tens of thousands of IDs mean hundreds of MB of copying per batch. Use a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt instead.

findings.title: Placeholder path can exceed MySQL/Postgres bind-parameter limits for large batch sizes
findings.body: On non-SQLite databases, each ID becomes a bound parameter. MySQL and Postgres cap prepared statements at 65535 parameters. If `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` is configured above that, the DELETE fails on every run and cleanup never progresses. The old subquery-based statement had no such limit. Either chunk the IDs or inline them for all dialects.
